title: [Perf][SM90] Score only candidate blocks in the DSv4.1 decode indexer
body:
## Overview

Add a Triton candidate-only decode scoring path for DeepSeek V4.1 on SM90,
reading FP8 K directly from the paged indexer cache instead of scoring the
full context and masking it afterwards.

Related to #61830. This is a separate implementation from the gather-based
prototype in draft #62000: it avoids the intermediate candidate-K buffer.
The flag is off by default (`VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_PAGED_DECODE=1` to enable).

## Claims

- On H20 TP8 with ~1M input tokens, the evalscope A/B below measured a
  **9.6–23.8% reduction in mean ITL** across concurrency 1/2/4/8.
- Consumer logits use 16,384 candidate columns instead of the full compressed
  context. The candidate-source layers, pre-candidate layers and prefill path
  are unchanged.
- Path selection uses configuration checks, not capture-time context lengths.
  Live lengths and page tables remain device inputs during CUDA graph replay.

These results cover the measured long-context workload, not a general
no-regression claim. Accuracy and shorter-workload checks are still pending.

## Validation

### Environment

- Machine: 8x NVIDIA H20 96GB, TP8; driver 535.161.08, CUDA 13.0
- Software: torch 2.14.0+cu130, triton 3.8.0, deep_gemm 2.8.1, vLLM at this
  PR's commit
- Server: `--tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 1048576 --max-num-seqs 16
  --enable-prefix-caching`, speculative decoding with
  `num_speculative_tokens=5`. The A/B runs differ only in
  `VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_PAGED_DECODE` (0 vs 1)

### Test guards

```bash
pytest -q tests/kernels/attention/test_candidate_paged_logits.py
```

The tests cover:

- **Scores and selection:** candidate logits against an FP32 reference
  (`rtol=2e-2`, `atol=1e-2`), plus selected-set comparisons for `persistent`
  and `auto` top-k. This is kernel-level coverage, not model accuracy.
- **Cache layout:** page gaps of 0/64/260 bytes with block sizes 16/64;
  invalid cache entry widths are rejected.
- **Bounds:** empty contexts, padded/out-of-range candidate blocks, and
  per-row causal limits during speculative decoding.
- **CUDA graphs:** capture on a short context, replay with changed lengths
  and page tables, then compare against eager execution.
- **Gating and workspace:** default-off behavior, rejected configurations,
  and reuse of the reserved workspace without growth during capture.
- **Performance smoke test:** an effective-bandwidth threshold over the
  candidate path, intended to catch severe regressions, not to measure
  isolated HBM bandwidth.

The current L4 attention CI job skips the SM90 GPU cases. A saved H20 pytest
report for the submitted revision is still needed; the coverage above does
not imply those cases passed in CI.

### End-to-end A/B (1M context)

I ran both configurations on the same commit with the same client arguments.
There is one run per configuration, with 2/4/8/16 measured requests at
concurrency 1/2/4/8 respectively. Set `MODEL` to the served model name and
`TOKENIZER_PATH` to the matching local checkpoint:

```bash
evalscope perf \
  --model "$MODEL" --api openai --stream --api-key EMPTY \
  --url http://127.0.0.1:8021/v1/chat/completions \
  --dataset random --tokenizer-path "$TOKENIZER_PATH" \
  --prefix-length 1028976 --min-prompt-length 1024 --max-prompt-length 1024 \
  --number 2 4 8 16 --parallel 1 2 4 8 --warmup-num 1 \
  --max-tokens 16384 --temperature 0.7 --top-p 0.95 --seed 42 \
  --extra-args '{"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}, "ignore_eos": true}'
```

The logs report 1,029,974 input tokens and 16,384 output tokens per request.
The configured prefix length is 1,028,976; input counts above are the measured
counts after prompt construction, not a sum of the CLI length arguments.
The tables report zero cached prompt tokens, but that alone does not verify
server-side prefix-cache hits, especially with this shared-prefix workload.

| Conc. | ITL avg (ms) dense -> cand | ITL p50 (ms) dense -> cand | ITL p90 (ms) dense -> cand |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 12.27 -> 11.09 (**-9.6%**) | 12.28 -> 11.14 (-9.3%) | 12.73 -> 11.73 (-7.9%) |
| 2 | 15.85 -> 13.68 (**-13.7%**) | 16.11 -> 13.50 (-16.2%) | 16.50 -> 14.37 (-12.9%) |
| 4 | 23.01 -> 18.31 (**-20.4%**) | 23.11 -> 18.81 (-18.6%) | 23.64 -> 19.47 (-17.6%) |
| 8 | 35.14 -> 26.78 (**-23.8%**) | 37.19 -> 27.05 (-27.3%) | 38.04 -> 27.88 (-26.7%) |

Secondary metrics from the same runs:

| Conc. | Decode toks/s | Spec. accept dense -> cand | TTFT avg (ms) dense -> cand |
| ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| 1 | +20.6% | 81.6% -> 83.0% | 4879.9 -> 4631.7 (-5.1%) |
| 2 | +30.1% | 81.7% -> 83.5% | 5822.9 -> 6107.6 (+4.9%) |
| 4 | +13.3% | 82.0% -> 80.8% | 8322.4 -> 7800.7 (-6.3%) |
| 8 | +21.5% | 81.8% -> 80.8% | 11900.4 -> 11179.7 (-6.1%) |

I use ITL as the main latency metric here, with TPOT and throughput as
supporting results. Under speculative decoding, streamed chunks can contain
multiple tokens: client ITL is not necessarily one GPU iteration, nor is it
independent of acceptance, scheduling or buffering. TPOT remains a valid
user-facing metric, but neither metric alone isolates the kernel change.

This is one A/B pair, not a confidence-interval result. Many intervals within
the same requests do not replace independent runs. At concurrency 4, overall
completion throughput was 827.33 -> 814.72 tok/s (-1.5%) despite lower ITL,
so this is not a throughput win at every concurrency.

I also ran an earlier TP4 test at 200K context. It showed a much smaller ITL
change; the TP8 evalscope run and trace below are the main evidence here.

### Kernel-level trace

The measurement record uses **PyTorch Profiler**, with 100 decode iterations
at ~1M context and client concurrency 12. On rank 0:

| Observation | Dense | Candidate-only |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Mean decode rows/step | 55.2 | 44.3 |
| Scoring time/call | 2027.0 us | 56.4 us |
| Candidate expansion + remap/call | — | 8.2 + 1.8 us |
| Candidate mask + flags, total | 68.10 ms | absent |
| Cooperative top-k time/call | 221.1 us | 94.2 us |

The dense scoring bucket groups the candidate source and four consumers;
the new scoring kernel runs only for the four consumers. All eight ranks
show the new kernel and no consumer mask kernel (400 scoring calls per rank).
This confirms that serving actually exercises the new path.

The batches differ, so these are attribution measurements, not a matched-load
speedup. Even dividing by row count does not fully remove differences in
occupancy and batch composition. End-to-end latency comes from evalscope,
not the profiler's summed CUDA time.

### Accuracy

Model-level accuracy results are pending. I'll compare the flag on and off
with lm-eval and add the results here before merge. Kernel tests alone do not
establish model accuracy. Other SM90 GPUs have not been tested.

## Details

The path prepares per-row candidate blocks and causal bounds, reads candidate
K directly through the page table, scores into a compact buffer, runs the
existing top-k, and remaps the selected columns to request-local positions.
It reuses candidate preparation and remapping from vLLM's SM100 sparse path.
FP8 dot products use FP32 accumulation; invalid columns are masked and valid
column counts are passed to top-k.

For the tested model, `index_head_dim=128`, `index_n_heads=32`,
`candidate_topk_blocks=2048`, `candidate_block_size=8`, and `index_topk=512`.
The compact FP32 logits buffer is `[rows, 16384]` (1.5 MiB at 24 rows).
With five speculative tokens, six decode rows represent one fully populated
request in the kernel input; this is not necessarily the client's concurrent
request count because scheduling and graph padding can change the batch.

The path requires SM90, an FP8 indexer cache, no DCP/PCP, and supported
candidate geometry. When disabled or rejected by the availability check, the
existing dispatch remains in use; existing unsupported combinations may still
raise errors. The gate has no batch-size or context-length profitability
threshold. Avoiding a K copy does not remove preparation, sorting, top-k and
remapping costs, so short-context performance still needs checking.

## What's next

- **Accuracy:** compare lm-eval results with the flag off and on.
- **Performance outside 1M:** benchmark shorter contexts, small batches and
  smaller real datasets to check for latency or throughput regressions.
- **Kernel work:** try a CUDA/CUTLASS implementation and compare it with
  Triton. I'll profile scoring, candidate preparation and top-k before
  deciding which part to optimize; there is no measured speedup for this yet.

I'd appreciate feedback on the implementation while I finish the accuracy and
short-workload checks. Those results still need to be confirmed before merge.
Prefill optimization is outside this PR.

---

title: [Feature] Integrate Cake kernels via FlashInfer: model-by-model tracker
body:
**End-to-end validation and issue reporting:** Our shape coverage and correctness have not yet been validated end to end in model serving. If you encounter (1) end-to-end accuracy degradation, (2) unsuitable API requirements, such as unnecessarily requiring contiguous inputs, or (3) faster kernel benchmarks but worse end-to-end performance because the shapes optimized by the kernel do not cover the actual model-serving workload, please open an issue and tag @yyihuang with the affected kernel, the missing or problematic shape(s), and relevant model/serving details or a reproducer. We will resolve reported issues within **6 hours**.

## Motivation

Track integration of Cake kernels already delivered through FlashInfer into SGLang, grouped by the models that requested them. The upstream inventory is [flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4254](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4254); model requirements below come from its subissues and the linked implementation PRs.

The proposed integration is through FlashInfer's public/prepared APIs. Each task should connect the relevant model operator, weight/cache layout, and execution mode to an eligible kernel, then measure the complete serving path. Upstream kernel benchmarks are useful starting points, not claims of SGLang end-to-end speedup.

**Snapshot: 2026-10-03 (UTC; October 2 in US Pacific); FlashInfer main [46340689a5ab](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/commit/46340689a5ab5665ab39f6281dac4d021d7ae94b).** “Merged” below means available in upstream FlashInfer, not necessarily in a released wheel or integrated here. Open follow-ups are explicitly marked and are not included in the merged coverage. Most listed kernels target SM100/SM103; exact architecture, SM-count, dtype, layout, and shape admission remain API-specific. Let the serving adapter retain its existing backend for configurations outside those contracts.

Notation: `T/M` = token rows, `B` = requests, `Q` = query tokens per request, `S` = KV length. MoE tuples are **(hidden size, expert intermediate size, number of experts, top-k)**; an intermediate size marked “local” is after TP sharding. Enumerated benchmark shapes are evidence points, not an assertion that every combination is supported.

## Integration and acceptance

- [ ] Pin a FlashInfer revision/release containing the required merged APIs and register backend selection at the existing operator boundary.
- [ ] Check the selected release branch separately: [#5978](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5978) is merged into `release-v0.7.1` only and reverts the BF16 head-dim-256 small-M speculative-decode route because of an intermittent B200 hang. This is a separate route from the E4M3/page-64 DCP entries below; a merge on the release branch does not establish a fix on main.
- [ ] Prepare weights, plans, output buffers, and workspaces before graph capture; account for changing request lengths, routing, state indices, and graph buckets.
- [ ] Validate each listed model/checkpoint, quantization recipe, TP/EP/CP configuration, and state/cache layout. Cover prefill, decode, speculative verification, ragged batches, and prefix-cache reuse where relevant.
- [ ] Compare against the current engine backend on model quality, TTFT, TPOT, throughput, and memory. Record the actual selected route and unsupported configurations before changing defaults.

SGLang already has model/operator boundaries for these families. Existing integration work is linked below so this tracker can be completed by extending or landing those changes.

## 1. Kimi-K3 / Kimi-K3-NVFP4 / Kimi-K3 vision

Requirements: [NVFP4 end-to-end #4568](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4568), [TP12 #4542](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4542), [ragged MLA/DCP #4658](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4658), [NVFP4 MLA #4644](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4644), [W4A8 SiTU #5156](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/5156).

Start from [`kimi_k3.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/models/kimi_k3.py) for KDA/MLA/LatentMoE and [`kimi_k3_vl.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/models/kimi_k3_vl.py) for the vision tower. Preserve the model's layer ordering, TP reductions, state-cache semantics, and ModelOpt checkpoint preparation.

| Integration task | Covered shape / contract | FlashInfer delivery / upstream status |
|---|---|---|
| KDA prefill and fused decode | D=128. Fused one-token decode includes H=8 for TP12, plus H=12/24/32/48/96; BF16/FP32 indexed recurrent states and width-4 convolution. Prefill consumes strided q/k/v views of packed `[T,3*H*128]` projection output without densification. Prefill checkpoint outputs are BF16; FP32 checkpoints and `checkpoint_state_indices` are not admitted by the Cake prefill route. Recurrent T=1 decode with explicit `cu_seqlens` is outside the explicit Cake contract; `auto` now respects that guard. | **Merged:** `recurrent_kda(..., backend="cake")` and `fused_kda_decode(..., backend="cake")`; [#5551](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5551), [#5846](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5846); selector/binding updates [#5901](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5901) and [#5919](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5919) preserve the public API and served shape contracts; explicit-`cu_seqlens` auto-dispatch fix [#5760](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5760); [API](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/kda.py). |
| Dense FP8 MLA and ragged/DCP MLA | Kimi latent=512, RoPE=64, E4M3 query/cache, page=64; registered H=12/96 decode and Q<=8 MTP paths. The separate var-Q DCP API accepts BF16 or FP8 query/cache, H<=128, registered pages 32/64/128, compact cumulative query lengths and rank-local KV metadata; returns BF16 output + FP32 natural-log LSE. Caller performs the cross-rank merge. | **Merged:** `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(..., backend="cake")`, [#5552](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5552), [#5627](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5627); `cake_mla_varq_dcp_decode`, [#5577](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5577). |
| FP8 dense projections | BF16 activations and ModelOpt E4M3 weights with 128x128 block scales. 22 TP1/TP8 projection families, evaluated at M={1,8,64,256,4096,16384}; hidden=7168, representative global K→N: 7168→49152 fused QKVG, 7168→1536 Q-A, 1536→18432 Q-B, 7168→576 KV-A, 512→24576 KV-B, 12288→7168 O. Prepare/repack weights once; preserve padding and valid output columns. | **Merged:** `flashinfer.gemm.kimi_k3_fp8_projection`, [API/shape guide](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/experimental/kimi_k3_fp8_projection/README.md), merged [#5642](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5642). |
| Fused router + expert-aligned route plan | FP32 logits `[M,896]`, top-16, sigmoid + selection bias, normalization of unbiased selected weights, deterministic lower-ID ties; block_m=8/16. **Current M admission is powers of two from 1 through 8192**, not arbitrary batches. | **Merged:** `kimi_k3_fused_router` / `prepare_kimi_k3_fused_router`; [#5531](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5531), [#5621](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5621), [contract](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/experimental/kimi_k3_fused_router/README.md). |
| LatentMoE front and tail, TP1/TP8 | BF16 input `[T,7168]` → router logits `[T,896]`, latent `[T,3584]`, shared SiTU `[T,6144/TP]`; tail reduces supplied routed partials, normalizes, projects to 7168 and combines shared output. T=1..128 decode, prefill validated through 16384. **148-SM devices only in this package**, TP1/8, no EP; final all-reduce remains caller-owned. | **Merged:** `flashinfer.kimi_k3_latent_moe` prepared front/tail APIs; merged [#5734](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5734), [contract](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/experimental/kimi_k3_latent_moe/README.md). |
| TP12 distributed LatentMoE tail | Routed latent `[M,3584]`, shared partial `[M,7168]`, reduce + norm + up-projection + shared reduction. Twelve GB200/GB300 NVL72 ranks in one NVLink domain; evaluated M=1..4096. Separate API/workspace from TP1/8; each rank must agree on M and workspace capacity. | **Merged:** `flashinfer.kimi_k3_tp12_tail`; [#5603](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5603), [#5668](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5668). |

Match each operator's topology and layout; evaluate multi-rank end-to-end behavior. | **Merged:** [#5512](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5512), [#5263](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5263), fused norm/combine [#5540](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5540). |

Examples include FP4 (N,K)=(4608,5120)/(5120,2304) and M={16,128,512,4096}; catalog-specific SM-count and dtype constraints. Integrate forward operators only where model geometry matches. | **Merged:** [#5523](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5523); mixed FP8/FP4 GEMM updates [#5739](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5739), [#5754](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5754), and gate update [#5766](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5766). | Ragged BF16 grouped GEMM for MoE expert forward projections | SM100/SM103/SM107. BF16 A[sum_M,K], B[E,N,K] → BF16 output; FP32 accumulation, N % 256 = 0, K % 64 = 0. Device int32 `m_indptr[E+1]` (or cumulative end offsets for the experimental API); imbalanced, empty and non-tile-aligned groups, no row padding or host offset readback. Prepared launch can reuse bound tensors after offsets/values change. | **Merged:** `flashinfer.grouped_mm.grouped_mm_bf16(..., backend="cake")` or `prepare_grouped_gemm_fwd(...).launch()`; [#5751](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5751), [API contract](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/docs/api/cake_moe_grouped_gemm.rst). This row covers forward only; qualify actual serving token/expert distributions. |
| Prepared generated MegaMoE, fixed 384-expert geometry | Separate from EP16 below: (H,I,E,top-k)=(5120,2304,384,6), packed FP4/FP8 and documented clamped-SwiGLU scale semantics. SM100 requires 148 physical SMs; SM103 requires 152. Registered FP4 T={1,16,128,512} (source family also 1024/4096), FP8 T=16. Unsupported shapes have no internal fallback. The `num_sms` override and smoke-only shapes were removed; captured pipeline `run()` is one kernel. New tests ran on B200; the available 148-SM B300 could not exercise the 152-SM catalog. |
| Hopper native BF16 expert-parallel MegaMoE | SM90/H100; BF16 dispatch, expert compute, intermediate, combine wire and output with FP32 accumulation/route weighting. H % 256 = 0, I % 128 = 0, top-k={1,2,4,6,8}, experts divisible by world size, one node, world<=32. Measured EP2/4/8 and T=8..4096 include (H,I,E,top-k)=(7168,2048,256,8), (7168,3072,384,6), (4096,2048,256,6); these do not establish coverage of every admitted configuration. Arbitrary routed-pair order, including expert-sorted dispatch. H=2688/3072, rank32, T<=2048 keeps specialized programs; other admitted shapes use generic bundles. Prepare pointer-stable buffers before graph use; current validation requires contiguous inputs. | **Merged:** `flashinfer.fused_moe.prepare_bgmv_moe(..., backend="cake", fallback=True)`, [#5850](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5850), portable fallback/current-stream fix [#5809](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5809); [API contract](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/fused_moe/bgmv_moe.py). Round-8 runtime evidence on SM90/SM100/SM103/SM107; capability-specific dispatch. Preserve per-request k/p and RNG semantics; deterministic replay within this backend does not imply identical token streams to every other sampler. | **Merged:** `flashinfer.cake_sampling`, [#5439](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5439), [#5731](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5731), round 7 [#5847](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5847) and latest round 8 [#5950](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5950) (same correctness/RNG contract); existing `flashinfer.sampling.softmax` dispatch, [#4282](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4282). | Block-sparse/VSA and Sage attention | VSA wrapper backend for supported sparse metadata; separate SM90 and SM100-family paths. Sage FP8 block-sparse on SM100/103 supports its documented ragged/GQA and scale contracts; SM120 INT8 is another portfolio. | **Merged:** [SM90 VSA #5687](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5687), [SM100 VSA #4593](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4593), [Sage FP8 #5442](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5442), [SM120 #5127](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5127). |

Motivation
DeepSeek-V4.1 verification rows from the same request score the same FP4 index-K cache. The existing Triton path decodes K independently for each query row; capacity-sized CUDA Graphs also leave substantial work on invisible positions.
This PR adds an opt-in SM90 grouped indexer that converts packed E2M1 to E5M2 in shared memory and uses FP8 WGMMA, reusing each decoded K tile across query rows. Hopper has no native MXFP4 MMA. The grouped path preserves the existing BF16 rounding points, ReLU, head weighting, and reduction order.
Changes
Optimize scale decoding in the existing SM90 Triton fallback.
Add a grouped CUDA path for H64/D128 request-major verification rows, with one query per warpgroup and shared K tiles of 64 positions.
Retain up to six decoded Q rows across 2/4/8 K tiles, with shape-dependent dispatch.
Compute
group_max_len
on device, skip completely invisible chunks/tiles, and write
-inf
. Partial tiles avoid reading invalid
req_to_token
entries.
Add a persistent scheduler: parallel device-side length loading, visible-chunk prefixes, a bounded resident CTA grid, and chunk sizing based on actual visible work. Q remains resident across assigned chunks from the same group.
Add a three-stage pipeline:
cp.async
loads packed tile i+2 while CUDA cores decode tile i+1 and WGMMA consumes tile i. Unaligned cache addresses retain a scalar-load fallback.
Extend registered tests for invisible tiles, partial groups, and CUDA Graph replay after changing lengths.
Dispatch and compatibility
fp4_index_logits_grouped_sm90(..., implementation=...)
accepts:
Value
Behavior
"auto"
(default)
Shape-dependent rectangular grid with Q residency and visibility skipping
"persistent"
Schedule visible chunks on a resident grid
"pipeline"
Persistent scheduling plus asynchronous packed-load/software-decode/WGMMA overlap
The grouped path remains opt-in; it is not enabled globally.
auto
does not automatically select persistent/pipeline. Measurements below show that the best mode depends on shape and visibility.
Scheduler metadata is CTA-local shared memory, recomputed on every invocation and graph replay. There is no CPU length readback, global allocation/counter, or request-slot scratch. Persistent modes support up to 1024 request groups and six rows per group, falling back to the single-tile path for larger inputs. Random physical slots, partial final groups, per-row lengths, compression ratios 1/2, and padded output/cache strides are supported.
Numerical behavior and resources
Packed FP4 block scales are factored into a common power-of-two scale, restored after FP8 accumulation, and followed by the existing BF16 dot rounding, ReLU, BF16 weighted-product rounding, FP32 head reduction tree, and final BF16 rounding.

SASS inspection confirms QGMMA issuance, subsequent packed LDGSTS and software decode, then WARPGROUP.DEPBAR. The final build has no WGMMA serialization warning. The pipeline does not consistently outperform serial persistent scheduling.
Validation
Executed on H20:
23 independent configurations: widths 1–1025, query group sizes 2/3/4/5/6/7/9, partial groups, pages 16/64, ratios 1/2, random physical slots, varying lengths including zero, padded strides and output guards. Applicable variants match the prior CUDA implementation bit for bit; an independent integer-dot oracle also matches.
Three registered tests pass through the real Python/custom-op/JIT entry, including all three implementations against Triton with changing graph-replay visibility.
Additional graph checks cover long → empty → short → long transitions, poisoned invisible slots and unaligned table strides; outputs match exactly.
Metadata-capacity/fallback checks at 257, 1024 and 1025 groups, and group size nine pass.
Full 23-case Compute Sanitizer memcheck/racecheck/synccheck: zero errors or hazards. Additional graph and metadata-boundary memcheck runs also pass.
Pre-commit checks pass, including registered-test validation.

Both paths receive identical FP4-representable BF16 Q, head weights, packed K, request mapping and visible lengths. Model-side fake quantization is shared upstream and excluded. title: [Tracking] GLM-5.3-Flash performance optimization on Hopper (SM90)
body:
<!-- Title: [Tracking] GLM-5.3-Flash performance optimization on Hopper (SM90) -->

This issue tracks performance work for GLM-5.3-Flash on NVIDIA Hopper (SM90) GPUs.

This list is part of the Q4 roadmap #42473 (Kernel optimization, PoC: @BBuf). Related: SM120 tracking #37813, GLM-5.3-Flash bug tracking #37524.

## DSA attention and indexer

- [x] Q8KV8 FP8 sparse prefill on GLM-5.3-Flash with BF16 KV cache — #41790
- [x] Support TileLang FP8 KV cache on CUDA — #42957
- [x] k-pool: 256-token logical page so index page id = logical page id — #42178
- [ ] Support the flashmla_sparse_q8 prefill backend on CUDA — #44217
- [ ] Unify the q8kv8 sparse-prefill topk_length source with the BF16 path — #36305
- [ ] Pick any divisor of the tile count for the TileLang sparse decode split — #45274
- [ ] Split top-k across CTAs for small CUDA BF16 TileLang sparse decode — #43917
- [ ] Support group-scaled FP8 NoPE KV reads for CUDA TileLang — #39349
- [ ] Add GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 KV cache on SM90 with FA3 — #45072

## KDA (linear attention)

- [x] Fuse GLM-5.3-Flash KDA projections and prefill metadata — #39688
- [x] Support ReplaySSM ring-write in the fused chain-verify kernel — #36821
- [x] Support Helion MTP verification and harden prefill, decode — #42857
- [ ] Extend the CuTe DSL MTP verify kernel to SM90 — #44612
- [ ] Defer accepted-state materialization for SM90 Triton verify — #39025
- [ ] Make KDA backend dispatch hardware- and shape-aware — #37901
- [ ] Run the KDA projection GEMMs in FP8 on SM90, extending [#38764](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38764) and [#44629](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44629) @JackChuang

## MoE and communication

- [x] Extend FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE autotune coverage to prefill chunks — #43363
- [x] Add H20 block-FP8 MoE configs for GLM-5.3-Flash EP4/EP8 — #38913
- [x] Support GLM-5.3-Flash with DeepEP v2 — #40466
- [ ] Add H20 fused_moe configs for GLM-5.3-Flash TP8/TP4 — #45089

## Speculative decoding (MTP / DFlash)

- [ ] Skip the per-rank eager-draft fallback for a missing DSA seed under DP attention — #41269
- [ ] Register the NextN draft's DSA index cache for hybrid linear-attention pools — #41334
- [ ] Allow PP + EAGLE/NEXTN prefill for Glm5Next — #41335
- [ ] Gather DFlash aux hidden states for every scattered MoE all-to-all backend @JackChuang
- [ ] Fill the MTP draft KV without attention for all but the last prompt token after prefill @JackChuang

## CUDA graph

- [ ] Init persistent cache for breaking modules in prefill breakable graph — #43776
- [ ] Enable breakable prefill CUDA graphs for GLM-5.3-Flash with prefill context parallel — #44293

## Fixes

Issue body actions
We are evaluating an MXFP4 x MXFP8 W4A8 GEMM on NVIDIA H100.
The fused-E8M0 Humming kernel is numerically correct, but with group-32
MXFP8 activation scales it is significantly slower than both:
Humming's generic group-scale path
A QDQ baseline that dequantizes both operands and then runs a BF16 GEMM
We would like to ask whether group-32 MXFP8 input scaling is an intended
performance target and whether there are plans to optimize this case on Hopper.
Quantization format
The operands use the following format:
Activation payload: FP8 E4M3
Activation scale: per-token, per-K-group power-of-two scale
Activation group size: 32
Weight payload: MXFP4 E2M1
Weight scale: E8M0
Weight group size: 32
Output dtype: BF16
This is an MXFP8-style activation representation: each 32-element K group
contains an E4M3 payload and one power-of-two scale.
Humming receives the decoded real FP32 activation scales through
input_scale
. The original activation scales are exactly representable
as E8M0 powers of two.
This differs from the DeepEP grouped-FP8 case added by
#37
:
PR
fix: support grouped FP8 MXFP4
#37
activation group size: 128
This case activation group size: 32
Both cases use MXFP4 weights with E8M0 group size 32
Environment
GPU: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3
Humming commit tested:
79c1cef
/
#35
Output dtype: BF16
Warmup: 20 iterations
Measurement: 200 iterations
Timing: CUDA events and CUDA Graph replay
GEMM operation count:
2 * M * N * K
PR
#37
was merged after the tested commit. Based on its diff, it adds the
group-128 integration and fixes non-fused scale tail decoding, but does
not appear to change fused WGMMA accumulator scheduling or the H100
heuristics. We can confirm the measurements on the latest main if needed.

For large-M shapes, the fused kernel reaches only approximately

Suspected bottleneck
Our current understanding is:
For FP8,
kPartMmaShapeK
is 32.
With
input_scale_group_size=32
, every WGMMA step reaches an activation
scale boundary.
scale_d
is therefore false at every K=32 step.
The current path performs
wgmma_commit()
followed by
wgmma_wait<0>()
, register fencing, and accumulator scaling for every
K=32 group.
The fused H100 heuristic selects a relatively large
128x128x128
base tile, which may increase the cost of processing the accumulator
at each group boundary.
With the group-128 input scales used by PR
#37
, four K=32 WGMMA operations
can accumulate before applying the activation scale. The synchronization
and accumulator-processing overhead can therefore be better amortized.
This is only our interpretation of the current implementation; please
correct us if we are missing another bottleneck.
Comparison with an experimental Gluon implementation
For reference, an experimental Gluon implementation reaches approximately
580-665 effective TFLOPS for the same large-M shapes.
That implementation performs one-time offline preprocessing of the static
MXFP4 weight into a cached FP8 weight tensor and therefore consumes an
additional
N * K
bytes of device memory. It is not a direct memory-footprint
comparison with Humming's packed-MXFP4 kernel, but it suggests that the
group-32 activation scaling itself does not necessarily prevent high
throughput if preprocessing extra static weight storage is acceptable.
We do not expect the packed-MXFP4 Humming kernel to match this result
without considering that memory tradeoff.
Questions
Is MXFP8 activation group size 32 an intended performance target for
Humming's fused-E8M0 W4A8 kernel?
Is the current implementation primarily optimized for group-128 input
scales such as the DeepEP format in PR
fix: support grouped FP8 MXFP4
#37
?
Are there plans to optimize the group-32 case on Hopper?
Would you recommend a different block/warp shape or disabling stream-K
for this workload?
Could an accumulator ring, delayed retirement, or another scheduling
strategy reduce the per-group
wgmma_wait<0>
overhead?
Would it be useful for us to provide the complete benchmark script,
Nsight Compute reports, or results from additional shapes?
Thank you.

This is because the combination of mixed‑precision quantization with group‑wise input quantization has a relatively low performance ceiling, it won't be much better than using BF16 activations.

Hi，the attachment contains the source code.
Core Kernels
1. _gluon_w4a8_mxfp8_accs_kernel
Processes one 32-element K group at a time:
WGMMA(A_fp8, W_fp8) -> FP32 partial
partial *= input_e8m0_scale
master += partial
This is the key to preserving numerical accuracy: the activation scale is applied to the FP32 partial accumulator, avoiding an additional rounding step from dequantizing and casting the activation back to FP8.
2. _gluon_w4a8_mxfp8_accs_batched_kernel
Loads multiple 32-element K groups in each TMA stage, typically using LOAD_K=128 or LOAD_K=256. This reduces TMA transactions, barrier overhead, and main-loop scheduling costs. It is the default high-performance path for large M.
3. _gluon_w4a8_mxfp8_splitk_kernel
Used for small M. It increases parallelism by distributing the K dimension across multiple CTAs. Each CTA accumulates into an FP32 temporary output using atomic additions, after which the result is converted to the requested output dtype.
4. _gluon_w4a8_mxfp8_prmt_kernel
A fallback path used when the WPREQ exactness guard fails. It uses prmt.b32 to fuse the decoding of packed MXFP4 weights with their weight scales into FP8 values. This path requires an offline T2 weight repacking step.
5. _gluon_w4a8_mxfp8_kernel
The most general but slower fallback path. It explicitly performs MXFP4 decoding, E8M0 scale application, and FP8 conversion inside the main loop.

Thank you. I manually performed some temporary local tuning and achieved only 500+ TFLOPs, which is lower than gluon. This is mainly because Humming's current implementation is not friendly to groupwise input scaling; a major optimization would require reimplementing a separate WGMMA path.
Additionally, I noticed a few issues with your code:
For the kernels under small batch sizes, you dequantize the input, multiply by the scale, and then quantize back to FP8. This is likely to cause serious precision problems, especially when the actual FP16 input values are very small (e.g., on the order of 0.001).
For the benchmarking script, you use CUDA Graphs. This may inflate the performance numbers for small batch sizes because the L2 cache is not flushed. I suggest using DeepGEMM's testing script instead.
https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1f6f3f378920ccb5cc036ef43eb3f5972e921713/deep_gemm/testing/bench.py#L79-L146

One cross-check from production serving on H200, same numeric recipe as this issue (MXFP4 e2m1/ue8m0-g32 weights × fp8 activations, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP4/EP4):
An A/B between humming's indexed MXFP4A8 and FlashInfer's CUTLASS sm90 MXFP4A8 (flashinfer #3738 via sglang #34967) came out at parity end-to-end, ~2137 vs ~2142 tok/s output median on identical protocol — details in
sgl-project/sglang#40417
.
Given the assessment above that a real fix needs a dedicated WGMMA path, the notable part is that an independent CUTLASS implementation lands in exactly the same place. That's consistent with groupwise-scale handling being a structural cost on Hopper across implementations, rather than something tuning on humming's side can recover. We also measured ~65% of peak memory bandwidth at decode-typical M for these shapes (analysis in 40417), which bounds what config-level work can gain.
